## What to do

* **Audit the scope before executing.** Treat the scope above as a starting point to extend, not a checklist to stay inside. Before running the review, look for what is *in-remit but unlisted*: surfaces this review should cover that the scope did not name. Fold them in. Examples to check include `public/` as a whole, `.github/`, `tests/` as a growth shape, `docs/plans/`, SD hotspots, and tracker signals (task age, cycle time, completion cadence) as a secondary surface. A scope you could only shrink is suspect; the expected move is to widen it to what the remit actually reaches. Stay **broad in discovery but bounded in output.** The wider scope changes only *what you examine*, not *what you report*. The report stays uncapped and severity-ranked; a clean, near-empty result is a genuine outcome. The no-follow-up rule below stays exactly as it is.
* **Read prior runs first. This review is trend-aware.** Read `stability-review-2026-11-04.md` in full, and `2026-10-21` / `2026-10-12` / the `2026-06-25` baseline as needed. Then frame every finding as a delta against the previous run: new, unchanged, improved, worsened or resolved, never a point-in-time snapshot. Stability is a *trajectory*: a single snapshot cannot tell convergence from a spiral, so the comparison against prior runs is the whole point.
* **Run the review.** Assess whether the project's rate of change is **converging toward a settled state or failing to settle**. Ground it in the change-history data available: `git log` over both repos, the CI run list, and lightweight tracker signals. Introduce **no new tooling** and no metrics product; run 4's scripts are reusable. Measure change in **relative** terms, normalised to the size and age of what changed, never as raw counts: a raw churn number says nothing, churn relative to the size and age of what it touches is the signal. Look at:
  * *churn hotspots*: areas re-touched far more than the rest, weighted by how much of them changes each time;
  * *trend over time*: is a hot area's churn settling as it matures, or flat-high / still climbing?;
  * *change-coupling*: areas that keep changing together, a sign their boundary has not settled;
  * *the overall convergence shape*: is the project's rate of change trending toward an asymptote, or not?

  Distinguish the cases that matter. Healthy early-stage churn is expected, not a finding, and healthy stabilisation is a maturing area going quiet. Set those against runaway instability (churn that should have settled but is flat-high or rising) and its opposite, stagnation (an area gone silent that should still be evolving). The discriminator is always the *trajectory of the relative rate*, judged against this project's own history, not an absolute threshold imported from elsewhere. These finding-classes are **examples, not a limit**. Discover the complete set for this remit from the repo; a class list is a floor to build on, never a ceiling to stay inside. Keep method 12 (split generated output from authored volume), and extend it wherever new generated volume appears.
* **Grounding caveat:** the trajectory research behind this review (relative change predicting instability, change-history decay indices, hotspot/trend analysis, reliability-growth convergence) comes overwhelmingly from human-team, long-lived systems, where change is slow and expensive. An agent-driven project churns far faster and differently. Do not import absolute thresholds from that work. Fold in the *shape* of the idea (relative change, trend over time, convergence toward a settled state) and calibrate every judgement against this project's own history.
* **Mind the altitude; do not double-flag.** This review works at the **project-trajectory / rate-of-change** altitude: is the whole project converging over time? That is distinct from the per-module Code Quality Review (complexity hotspots weighted by risk × churn at a point in time) and the cross-cutting Drift & Coherence Review (whether the code's structure is drifting apart). Do not re-flag what those own: a single complex module or a single duplication is theirs. Your finding is a *pattern in the rate of change over time*.
* **Write an uncapped, trend-framed report.** The deliverable is a clear, severity-ranked report of everything found. Finding nothing, one thing or several are all valid. Do not pad, cap or invent make-work to hit a number; a clean "still converging" result is a genuine outcome. Ground each finding against the change history at HEAD, not prior prose. Close with a compact **trend ledger**: each signal under a stable, descriptive name, with its severity and its delta against the 2026-11-04 run, so the next run can compare mechanically. Record the report at `docs/reviews/stability-review-YYYY-MM-DD.md`, with evidence in `docs/reviews/_evidence-YYYY-MM-DD/`; confirm that convention before you start writing. If discovery genuinely turns up no such place, put the full report in a comment on this task instead of inventing a new location.
* **Report back for a human decision; mint NO follow-up tasks.** This review is the governor: its conclusion is an *assessment a human acts on*, not auto-generated work. Do NOT create follow-up tasks, and do NOT write area notes. End the report with a plain-language read of the trajectory: where the project is converging, and where it is spiralling or stagnating. Give the options a maintainer might weigh: consolidate or freeze a thrashing area, slow the rate of new change, or investigate why an area will not settle. Leave the decision to them. A brake that spawned more work would be adding throttle, not braking.
* **Stay review-only.** Producing the report changes no code, config or secrets, and no docs beyond the report artifact and its evidence directory. An operator instruction to avoid touching files is about the code and docs *under review*. It does not override this task's own deliverable, and the report artifact is never the code under review.
* **Get a fresh-context adversarial second-read before this task can conclude.** This is a required, structural step, not advice. After the report is written, and before the Done transition can succeed, a genuinely separate reader must answer one question cold: *"what is the largest item in this window that this report missed or misfiled?"* Two tiers count as separate enough:
  * **Tier 1 (preferred):** dispatch a wholly separate session with no memory of this run.
  * **Tier 2 (accepted fallback):** a fresh-context sub-agent carrying no memory of the report-writing turn.
  * **Tier 3 is not accepted:** this same session re-reading its own report "from a cold stance".

  State which of Tier 1 or Tier 2 you used. Then post **one comment** on this task with these three fields together in a single comment body:
  * `Adversarial second-read verdict: AGREE` or `Adversarial second-read verdict: DISAGREE`;
  * `Differed from top finding: YES` or `Differed from top finding: NO`: whether the reader's own answer to the largest-missed-item question differed from the report's own top-ranked finding, independent of the verdict;
  * `Disposition: fixed in place`, `Disposition: escalated`, or `Disposition: no change`.

  That comment is mandatory, not optional documentation. The engine reads it and refuses a premature Done transition, naming exactly what is missing, until all three fields are present together in one comment body. Copy the same three fields into a `## Adversarial Second-Read` section of the report itself, with the tier used, the question, and the reader's answer in full. That section is a human-readable duplicate the engine never reads, not a substitute for the comment. **AGREE and DISAGREE both conclude this task normally. A DISAGREE verdict is itself the escalation**, visible in the comment and the appendix, never a reason to leave this task open pending a human.
* **Merge your own report PR.** Open one docs-only PR with the report and its evidence. Once its required CI checks (`ci-success`) are green, merge it before the Done transition; the report is docs-only, so merging it yourself is safe. Only when merging is genuinely impossible (no merge permission, required checks still red) may this task conclude with that PR left open. In that case, hand it off explicitly by naming what blocks the merge in the closing comment, never as ordinary completion. An open, not-yet-merged report PR is not a normal terminal state. Escalating, whether through a DISAGREE verdict or a named merge blocker, never blocks concluding.
* **Then conclude this task; do not leave it open.** Post a concise, severity-ranked summary of the report as a comment on this task, with a GitHub blob, commit or PR link to the full report (or the full report itself if it has no separate location). Then move the task to Done. Concluding is the whole point: a review task left open is re-recommended for review indefinitely and never resolves.

### Direction, and what was set aside

The report is written from measurements this session runs itself at one pinned endpoint; the research comment's figures (LV `9574d537`, 114 landings, SD `5d8489e`, 20 landings) are the expected values, not inputs.

* **Pin once, never splice.** First step: fetch both repos and record LV and SD `origin/main`. Writing research numbers beside rerun ones would mix two endpoints. Record both SHAs, with timestamps, in the evidence README. The report's own PR lands after the pin and is outside the window, as run 4's landings were the start of this one.
* **Parameterised copies of run 4's scripts.** Copy `measure_lv.py`, `measure_lv_cluster.py` and `measure_ci.py` once; endpoints come from argv/env, and the `{RUN3_END}..HEAD` range must use the passed SHA (the research spike changed exactly that). The report must say why it counts as a stability signal rather than bookkeeping: it is the review layer's own rate of change, it is not converging, and nothing caps or indexes it.
